title: Service Entry Sheet Invoicing: Why Service Suppliers Get Paid Weeks Later Than Goods Suppliers
summary: Service suppliers cannot invoice until the buyer approves a service entry sheet. Learn why SES approval lag drives DSO and how to automate the chain.
body_markdown:
**TL;DR:** If you sell services rather than goods, your invoice is gated by a document you may not control: the service entry sheet. Until the buyer approves it, the invoice cannot be raised in their AP portal, so a receivable sits idle for weeks while your ageing report starts the clock at invoice date. The fix is to measure approval lag as its own stage, raise the sheet yourself where the buyer allows it, and automate submission and status tracking across every portal.


Most accounts receivable programmes assume that once work is done, an invoice can go out. For goods that holds: ship the pallet, collect the goods receipt, raise the invoice.


For services — manpower, maintenance, facilities, logistics handling, engineering, professional work — it does not hold. A document sits between delivery and invoicing that most AR dashboards never show: the service entry sheet. Because it lives on the buyer’s side, suppliers often cannot see it, chase it, or measure it. The result is a category of days sales outstanding that looks like a collections problem but is an acceptance problem. No dunning fixes it, because the invoice that would be chased does not exist yet.


## What Is a Service Entry Sheet, and Why Does It Sit Between You and Payment?


A service entry sheet records which services were actually performed against a service purchase order, and at what value. It is the buyer’s formal acceptance of the work.


In SAP and SAP Ariba environments,[the procurement of services process](https://learning.sap.com/courses/procurement-process-overview/describing-the-procurement-of-services-in-sap-ariba) treats the sheet as a distinct object: each references a single purchase order, carries standard items for planned services or limit items for unplanned ones, and may be approved manually or automatically. Crucially, the supplier invoice is created *after* the sheet is approved — the approved sheet becomes the reference document. The sheet is not overhead on top of invoicing; it is a precondition for it.


Stage Goods supplier Service supplier


Delivery evidence Physical arrival, counted Hours or milestones, asserted


Acceptance artefact Goods receipt note Service entry sheet


Who creates it Receiving team, as routine Requisitioner or supplier, as an extra task


Invoice may be raised On or near delivery Only after sheet approval


Every row in the right-hand column adds variance, and variance compounds.


## Why Do Service Suppliers Get Paid Later Than Goods Suppliers?


Nobody on the buyer side is measured on approving your entry sheet. A goods receipt is created by a function whose purpose is to receive. A sheet is approved by an operations manager or site engineer measured on uptime and delivery — for whom your paperwork is admin.


Nor is this a minor segment of spend. Research summarised by industry press puts services at roughly a third of total organisational spend on average, as high as 86% in some organisations, while noting that capability to source and manage services lags well behind goods procurement.


Three mechanics drive the lag:


1. **Authoring friction.** If the buyer must create the sheet before approving it, two tasks sit with a busy person instead of one. Suppliers who raise it themselves remove the authoring step — and buyers can upload sheets on behalf of suppliers in Ariba Network.
2. **Evidence lag.** Sheets need a timesheet, job card, or completion certificate. If field teams submit paperwork weekly, the sheet waits.[Moving service confirmation online](https://www.supplyon.com/en/blog/getting-suppliers-to-enter-their-services-performed-online-reduces-the-cost-of-your-purchasing-process/) at the point of performance attacks this directly.
3. **Silent queues.** Portal notifications get filtered, misrouted, or sent to someone who left. The supplier reads silence as progress; the sheet sits unopened.


## Where Does the Chain Break, and What Does the Delay Cost?


The invoice is the *last* link in the chain, not the first — which is why measuring from invoice date hides most of the delay. Seven stages sit between service completion and an approved invoice, and five are on the supplier side. The belief that service payment delay is a buyer problem is mostly wrong: it is a supplier process problem with a buyer bottleneck in the middle.


Two failure modes are self-inflicted and expensive. The first is **invoicing from internal records rather than the approved sheet.** If an approver trimmed six hours and your invoice shows the original figure, the portal rejects it at validation — so you spend the approval wait *and* restart a rejection cycle. Disagreement over trimmed lines is a separate commercial conversation, not something to resolve by resubmitting a number the buyer declined. This is the same class of problem as[portal business rules that reject technically valid invoices](https://peakflo.co/blog/edi-invoice-exceptions-rejections-automation) .


The second is **batching.** If a sheet is approved on the 3rd and billing runs on the 30th, 27 days of accepted, uncontested receivable sat idle by internal policy — not a buyer delay. We have covered how[the gap between completion and customer visibility consumes working capital](https://peakflo.co/blog/invoice-delivery-gap-working-capital-dso-reduction) ; the entry sheet gate widens it substantially.


None of this appears in DSO reporting, because DSO conventionally starts at invoice date. If the sheet took 18 days to approve and the invoice was paid in 30, the report shows 30 and the business concludes collections are performing well. The table below models the true cycle for an illustrative services supplier — scenario arithmetic for comparison, not benchmark data.


Stage Manual services billing With entry sheet discipline


Completion to confirmation captured 7 days (weekly batch) 1 day (same-day capture)


Confirmation to sheet raised 4 days Same day


Sheet raised to approved 12 days (unchased) 5 days (tracked with SLA)


Approval to invoice raised 14 days (monthly run) Same day (event triggered)


Invoice submitted to approved 9 days (one rejection cycle) 4 days (matched to sheet)


**Total** **46 days** **11 days**


Thirty-five days of cycle time is a material working capital swing, and almost none of it comes from the buyer paying more slowly. Late payment is a documented drag on suppliers, which is why jurisdictions created oversight bodies such as[the UK Small Business Commissioner](https://www.gov.uk/government/organisations/small-business-commissioner) . Research from advisers including[The Hackett Group](https://www.hackettgroup.com/insights/) identifies process friction, rather than unwillingness to pay, as a primary driver of cash tied up in receivables, and treasury surveys from[the AFP](https://www.afponline.org/training-resources/resources/survey-research-economic-data) point to forecasting difficulty when collection timing is variable.


## Why Can’t Service Suppliers Just Fix This With an API or EDI?


Buyer AP portals are built for buyers, governed by the buyer’s procurement and IT functions, and the supplier is a guest. Supplier-facing APIs for raising entry sheets are rare, and where integration capability exists it usually needs a project on the buyer’s side — budget, IT resource, roadmap queue. A mid-sized supplier asking fifty enterprise customers each to run one will not get fifty yes answers.


E-invoicing mandates do not close the gap either. Frameworks such as[Peppol](https://peppol.org/) standardise how an invoice is structured and transmitted once it exists. They say nothing about whether the buyer accepted the underlying service. A mandate can make delivery instantaneous and leave an 18-day sheet queue intact.

## How Do Limit Items and Unplanned Services Make It Worse?


Planned services are the easy case: the purchase order specifies lines, and sheets consume them predictably. Unplanned services use limit items, where the buyer sets a ceiling value because exact scope is not knowable upfront — reactive maintenance, call-out work, variable-scope engineering. Each approved sheet consumes part of the limit, but nothing in the supplier’s systems tracks the remaining balance, because the limit lives in the buyer’s purchase order. Submissions exceeding the ceiling are blocked, discovered at submission time, after the work is done and unbillable until the buyer raises the limit — a request that goes back into a procurement queue.


Practical mitigations:


- Track consumed and remaining limit value per purchase order on your side, reconciled at each submission.
- Flag any purchase order at 80% consumption and request the increase before the limit binds.
- Watch validity dates as closely as values; an expired purchase order blocks submission just as firmly.
- Record who approves limit increases — frequently a different person from the sheet approver.


Suppliers whose source of truth is a timesheet or field service system rather than an ERP face an extra mapping layer, which we unpack in[invoice delivery for staffing agencies](https://peakflo.co/blog/staffing-agency-invoice-delivery-client-portals-automation) .


## What Should You Measure?


Stop measuring one number and measure the chain. If entry sheet lag is invisible, it cannot be managed.


Metric Definition


Confirmation capture lag Completion to signed confirmation in hand


Sheet authoring lag Confirmation received to sheet submitted


Sheet approval lag Sheet submitted to buyer approval, per customer


Approval to invoice lag Approval to invoice submitted in portal


Sheet rejection rate Rejected sheets as share of submissions


Invoice-to-sheet match rate Invoices matching approved values first time


True services cycle time Completion to invoice approved


Reporting approval lag *by customer* changes commercial conversations. An account averaging 22 days is not a collections issue to escalate at month end — it is a relationship issue for the account owner, with evidence. Routing those exceptions to someone accountable is its own discipline, covered in[exception ownership across distributed account teams](https://peakflo.co/blog/invoice-rejection-triage-routing-account-managers-portals) . When automating, sequence by volume, following[the 80/20 rule for portal automation](https://peakflo.co/blog/80-20-rule-portal-automation-ariba-coupa-first) .

## Our Verdict: Treat the Entry Sheet as a Billing Stage, Not Paperwork


Entry sheet lag is the most under-measured driver of services DSO — and most of it is addressable without asking a single customer to change anything.


### Act on this now if


- Services are a meaningful share of revenue and buyers mandate portal submission
- Your DSO looks acceptable but cash collection feels slower than the report suggests
- You run monthly billing against work that is accepted continuously
- Unplanned or call-out work sits on limit-item purchase orders you do not track
- More than ten active buyer portals are in play


### Lower priority if


- You sell goods almost exclusively and goods receipts confirm within a day or two
- Nearly all customers accept email invoices with no portal or acceptance gate
- Your services book is concentrated in two or three accounts with fast approvers


**Our recommendation:** start with measurement, not software. Instrument the chain for one quarter, splitting confirmation lag, authoring lag, approval lag, and approval-to-invoice lag into separate numbers per customer. In most services books the largest recoverable block is not the buyer’s approval queue — it is the batching policy holding approved work until the next billing run, and that one is entirely yours to change. Then automate the stages that scale worst: sheet submission, status tracking, and invoice delivery. Prove it on your two highest-volume portals before extending to the long tail.


## Conclusion


Services receivables fail differently from goods receivables, and most AR tooling was designed for the goods case. The service entry sheet is a genuine acceptance gate, and because it sits in the buyer’s system and is approved by someone with other priorities, it introduces delay that conventional DSO reporting is structurally blind to.


Suppliers who fix this do two unglamorous things. They measure the chain stage by stage instead of trusting a blended figure, and they own every stage they control — same-day confirmation capture, raising the sheet themselves where permitted, tracking limit consumption, invoicing off the approval event, and matching invoices to approved values. Automating submission and status tracking then removes the headcount ceiling.


The receivable was never waiting on the customer’s willingness to pay. It was waiting on a document nobody was watching.


## Frequently Asked Questions


### What is a service entry sheet?


A service entry sheet records which services were actually performed against a service purchase order and confirms their scope and value. It is the buyer’s formal acceptance of the work. In SAP and SAP Ariba environments each sheet references one purchase order, and invoice processing proceeds only once it is approved.


### Why can a supplier not invoice before the service entry sheet is approved?


Because the approved sheet is the evidence the buyer’s finance team relies on to treat the invoice as payable. Without it there is no accepted value to match against, so the invoice either cannot be created in the portal or is rejected at validation. The sheet is the services equivalent of the goods receipt in[three-way matching](https://peakflo.co/blog/ai-agents-three-way-matching-purchase-order-reconciliation-guide) .


### What is the difference between a service entry sheet and a goods receipt note?


A goods receipt note is generated when physical goods arrive and are counted — an observable event. A service entry sheet records intangible effort such as hours, visits, or milestones, and depends on a manager agreeing the work matches what was requested. That judgement step is why sheets stall far more often.


### How long does service entry sheet approval usually take?


It varies widely because the approver is an operational manager, not a finance user with a payables queue. Suppliers commonly see two days to several weeks, with the longest delays clustering around month end and accounts where the named requisitioner changed role. The variability matters more than the average, because unpredictable lag is what makes cash forecasting unreliable.


### Can a supplier create the service entry sheet themselves?


On many buyer configurations yes, and it is strongly to the supplier’s advantage. When the supplier raises the sheet the buyer only approves rather than authors it, removing a step nobody on the buyer side is measured on. The first question on any new service account should be who creates it.


### What are limit items and why do they cause rejections?


Limit items cover unplanned services where exact scope is unknown at purchase order creation, so the buyer sets a maximum value instead of fixed lines. Rejections happen when cumulative sheets exceed that ceiling, because the portal blocks anything above the remaining limit. Suppliers who do not track consumed limit value find out only when a submission fails.


### Does e-invoicing or Peppol solve the service entry sheet problem?


No. E-invoicing standardises how an invoice is transmitted once it exists, but the entry sheet gate sits earlier and governs whether the invoice may be raised at all. A mandate can make delivery instant and leave the approval delay untouched.


### How can a supplier track service entry sheet status across multiple buyer portals?


Manual tracking means logging into each portal on a schedule and transcribing status into a spreadsheet, which breaks down past roughly ten active accounts. The scalable approach is software that reads status from every portal on a cadence and surfaces only exceptions, so the team works one ageing queue — the same principle as[the long tail of non-standard invoice destinations](https://peakflo.co/blog/long-tail-client-portals-spreadsheets-custom-invoice-delivery) .


### What is the single biggest cause of service invoice rejection?


A mismatch between the invoice and the approved entry sheet, most often because the invoice was raised from internal billing records rather than approved sheet values. If an approver trimmed hours, the invoice must reflect the approved figure, and any difference is a separate commercial conversation.


### Can AI automate service entry sheet submission and invoice delivery?


Yes. An AI browser agent can log into buyer portals the way a person does, raise the sheet against the correct purchase order line, monitor approval status, and submit the matching invoice once approval lands. This matters because buyer portals rarely expose a supplier API, so interface-level automation is often the only route.[Service requisition and entry sheet handling](https://learning.sap.com/courses/creating-requisitions-in-sap-ariba-buying-and-invoicing/maintaining-service-requisition-details) differs enough between buyers that per-customer rules beat one generic workflow.
